pos: adj., superlative. (most goodly; fairest or most excellent in appearance)
etymology: Superlative of goodly, from Old English godlic, of good appearance; good + the adjectival -ly, carried by -est into the superlative of visible excellence.
biblical_def:
And he will take your menservants, and your maidservants, and your goodliest young men, and your asses, and put them to his work.

Samuel is pronouncing to Israel the true cost of the king they have demanded in his place. The word names the pick of the litter, not merely the good but the visibly best, the ones a man would least wish to surrender. That the king lays his hand precisely on the goodliest, rather than the least useful, is Samuel's whole point: a human kingship established apart from the LORD's own rule does not content itself with a nation's dregs but claims its best for its own purposes. Ben-hadad's demand of Ahab in 1 Kings 20 extends the same logic from persons to households: thy wives also and thy children, even the goodliest, are mine. Tyranny does not stop at tribute; it reaches for whatever is most prized. Scripture does not condemn goodliness itself, which it elsewhere praises, but it exposes what happens when the goodliest of a people becomes a resource for another man's appetite rather than a trust kept under God. The warning stands behind every later chapter of Israel's monarchy: a throne not bounded by covenant law will, sooner or later, requisition the best a people has, their sons, their fields, their inheritance, and call it merely due.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from GOODLY: superlative of goodly; of the finest, most comely, or most excellent appearance, the choicest in looks or quality.
webster_full: GOODLY, a. Being of handsome form; pleasant; agreeable to the eye.
GOODLIEST is its superlative: most goodly, most excellent in appearance.
1 Samuel 8: the king will take the goodliest young men for his own work.
1 Kings 20: Ben-hadad claims even the goodliest wives and children as his own.
Applied to whatever in a nation or household is most prized, and so most exposed to a tyrant's claim.
scriptures: And he will take your menservants, and your maidservants, and your goodliest young men, and your asses, and put them to his work.
Thy silver and thy gold is mine; thy wives also and thy children, even the goodliest, are mine.
corruption_summary: The word itself carries no live postmodern battle; it has simply fallen out of ordinary speech.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Goodliest has fallen out of ordinary speech, displaced by finest or best-looking, and carries no controversy to recover it from.

The principle behind it is still worth recovering: every tyranny, ancient or modern, civil or ecclesiastical, is known by what it claims as its own, not the useless or the surplus, but the goodliest of what a people has. Samuel's warning remains the test of any power that asks a people to surrender their best rather than merely their excess.
roots_summary: From Old English godlic, good in form, carried by the superlative suffix -est into a single English word for most excellent in appearance.
roots_lines: Goodly, from Old English godlic, names a handsome or comely form.
Goodliest is its superlative, the most excellent in appearance of a group.
1 Samuel 8 applies it to the young men a king will seize for his own work.
1 Kings 20 applies it to the wives and children a conqueror claims as tribute.
Both uses expose the same principle: power unchecked claims a people's best, not their least.
usage: the goodliest young men — Samuel's warning of what a king will requisition
even the goodliest, are mine — Ben-hadad's claim upon Ahab's household
a word now displaced by finest or best-looking in ordinary speech

pos: adv. (in a manner exciting horror; dreadfully)
etymology: From Latin horribilis, dreadful, from horrere, to bristle, shudder, stand on end with dread; the adverb names a fear that seizes the body, not merely the mind.
biblical_def:
Be astonished, O ye heavens, at this, and be horribly afraid, be ye very desolate, saith the LORD.

The LORD here summons the heavens themselves as witness against Israel, calling even inanimate creation to be horribly afraid at what His covenant people have done, forsaking the fountain of living waters for broken cisterns of their own hewing. The word names a dread that goes beyond ordinary fear, a shuddering appropriate to beholding something monstrous: not danger merely, but apostasy, a creature's abandonment of its own Creator. Ezekiel uses the same word for the nations who watch Tyre's fall, their kings shall be horribly afraid for thee, when I shall brandish my sword before them, trembling at every moment for their own life. In both places horribly describes the right response to the LORD's visible judgment on sin, whether Israel's covenant unfaithfulness or a proud city's collapse. Scripture does not treat such dread as excessive; it treats the absence of it, Israel's unastonished indifference to her own idolatry, as the deeper horror. The heavens can be horribly afraid at sin in a way that hardened human hearts frequently are not, which is itself the prophet's indictment.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from HORRIBLE: in a manner to excite horror; dreadfully; so as to cause shuddering dread.
webster_full: HORRIBLE, a. Exciting horror; dreadful; fearful in the highest degree.
HORRIBLY, adv. In a manner to excite horror; dreadfully.
Jeremiah 2: the heavens themselves are summoned to be horribly afraid at Israel's apostasy.
Ezekiel 32: the kings of the nations are horribly afraid at Tyre's judgment.
Names dread proper to witnessing covenant-breaking or divine judgment, not ordinary alarm.
scriptures: Jer 2:12
Be astonished, O ye heavens, at this, and be horribly afraid, be ye very desolate, saith the LORD.

Yea, I will make many people amazed at thee, and their kings shall be horribly afraid for thee, when I shall brandish my sword before them; and they shall tremble at every moment, every man for his own life, in the day of thy fall.
corruption_summary: No live postmodern redefinition attaches to the word; the recoverable principle is the loss of holy dread itself.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Horribly has simply narrowed to intensify trivial complaints, a horribly long line, with no controversy over its meaning to correct.

The principle Jeremiah presses is still urgent: a generation that cannot be horribly afraid at its own sin has lost something the heavens themselves are summoned to feel. The fear of the LORD, not a vague unease but the shudder proper to beholding apostasy, is precisely what a therapeutic age trains itself out of.
roots_summary: From Latin horrere, to bristle or shudder, through horribilis, the adverb names a bodily dread, not a mild unease.
roots_lines: Horrere, Latin for to bristle or shudder, is the word's deepest root.
Horribilis names what rightly excites that shudder: the dreadful.
Jeremiah 2 summons the heavens to be horribly afraid at Israel's apostasy.
Ezekiel 32 applies it to kings trembling at Tyre's judgment.
Both uses treat such dread as the fitting response to visible divine judgment.
usage: be horribly afraid — the heavens summoned as witness against Israel's apostasy
their kings shall be horribly afraid for thee — dread at Tyre's fall
a word narrowed today to mere intensifier, stripped of its dread

pos: adv. (in a manner deserving abhorrence; detestably)
etymology: From Latin abominari, to deprecate as an ill omen, from ab, away, + omen; the word that began as turning from a bad sign came to name conduct that turns the stomach of heaven itself.
biblical_def:
And he did very abominably in following idols, according to all things as did the Amorites, whom the LORD cast out before the children of Israel.

This is the Spirit's verdict on Ahab, a king who married Jezebel, built a house for Baal, and led Israel into the very idolatry for which the Amorites had already been dispossessed of the land. Abominably measures Ahab's idolatry not against a sliding moral scale but against the standard that condemned the nations Israel had replaced: he sinned as badly as the people the LORD had already judged unfit to keep the land. The adverb intensifies did, naming not a single lapse but a settled course of life. What makes the word theologically precise is the memory built into it, Ahab did not invent new evil but repeated an old one, under greater covenant light than the Amorites ever had. Israel was given the land on the express understanding that the nations before her were cast out for exactly this; Ahab's history therefore reads as Israel re-enacting the very judgment her own possession of Canaan was meant to be a verdict against. Scripture's harshest adverbs are reserved for sins that repeat, under more light, what was already condemned under less.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from ABOMINABLE: in an abominable manner; odiously; detestably; so as to excite abhorrence.
webster_full: ABOMINABLE, a. Odious in the highest degree; detestable; deserving abhorrence.
ABOMINABLY, adv. In an abominable manner; so as to excite abhorrence.
1 Kings 21: Ahab did very abominably in following idols.
Measured against the Amorites, already judged and cast out for the same sin.
Names a settled course of idolatry, not a single lapse.
scriptures: And he did very abominably in following idols, according to all things as did the Amorites, whom the LORD cast out before the children of Israel.
corruption_summary: No live postmodern redefinition attaches; the recoverable principle is repeating under greater light what was already condemned under less.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The word has simply gone out of common use, replaced by milder synonyms with none of its weight.

The principle still convicts: a church that has received more covenant light than Ahab ever had can still re-enact his very idolatry, trading the LORD for whatever Baal the age offers, and call it progress rather than the abominable repetition Scripture names it.
roots_summary: From Latin abominari, to turn away from as an ill omen, the word moved from ritual aversion to moral verdict: conduct heaven itself turns from.
roots_lines: Abominari, Latin for to turn from as a bad omen, is the deep root.
Abominable names what rightly provokes that turning-away: the detestable.
1 Kings 21 applies the adverb to Ahab's settled course of idol-following.
He is measured against the Amorites, already cast out for the same sin.
The word marks repetition, under greater light, of what was already condemned.
usage: did very abominably in following idols — the Spirit's verdict on Ahab
measured against the Amorites, already judged for the identical sin

pos: adj. (not keeping faith; treacherous or unreliable in trust)
etymology: From un-, a negative prefix, + faithful, from Old English faeth, faith, trust; the word names the breach of a bond that faithful presumes will hold.
biblical_def:
Confidence in an unfaithful man in time of trouble is like a broken tooth, and a foot out of joint.

Solomon's proverb measures unfaithfulness by what it costs precisely when it is most needed. A broken tooth fails at the moment of biting down; a foot out of joint fails at the moment of bearing weight. Confidence placed in an unfaithful man behaves the same way, it does not simply disappoint in the abstract, it collapses under the exact pressure it was trusted to bear, in time of trouble. The proverb is not chiefly about minor social unreliability but about covenant-shaped trust, the kind a man stakes his safety on, and what happens when the one trusted turns out hollow at the point of testing. Scripture elsewhere applies the same category to Israel's relation to the LORD, a people unfaithful to a covenant that was never meant to buckle under pressure, and to the LORD's own faithfulness as the standing contrast, He abideth faithful even when we believe not. Solomon's image supplies the ache behind every later indictment of covenant-breaking: trust given is trust that expects to bear weight, and an unfaithful man, like a broken tooth, is discovered precisely when weight is applied.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from FAITHFUL: not faithful; not observant of promises, duty, or allegiance; treacherous.
webster_full: FAITHFUL, a. Firm in adherence to promises, duty, or allegiance.
UNFAITHFUL, a. Not faithful; violating trust; treacherous.
Proverbs 25: confidence in an unfaithful man fails like a broken tooth, in time of trouble.
Trust is measured by what it bears under pressure, not merely in calm.
Stands in contrast throughout Scripture to the LORD's own unfailing faithfulness.
scriptures: Confidence in an unfaithful man in time of trouble is like a broken tooth, and a foot out of joint.
corruption_summary: A therapeutic age has quietly relocated faithfulness from covenant duty to felt authenticity, which an unfaithful heart can always claim to have.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern relational language increasingly measures faithfulness by sincerity of feeling rather than kept covenant: a spouse or a believer who breaks trust but felt genuine at the time is excused as merely following their truth, not named unfaithful at all.

Solomon's proverb will not allow the substitution. Faithfulness is proven exactly where sincerity is cheapest to claim, in time of trouble, under the weight trust was meant to bear. A broken tooth does not become whole because the mouth that broke it meant well; an unfaithful man is known by what fails under pressure, not by what he felt while failing.
roots_summary: Faith, from Old English faeth, names a bond of trust; the negative prefix un- marks its breach, a bond that was supposed to hold and did not.
roots_lines: Faeth, Old English for faith or trust, underlies faithful.
The prefix un- marks the negation: a bond that did not hold.
Proverbs 25 measures unfaithfulness by failure under pressure, not mere disappointment.
Confidence in such a man is like a broken tooth, a foot out of joint.
Stands throughout Scripture against the LORD's own faithfulness as the fixed contrast.
usage: confidence in an unfaithful man — trust that fails under pressure, not before it
like a broken tooth, and a foot out of joint — failure at the point of need
measured against the LORD's own unfailing faithfulness

pos: adv. (with reverent dread; in a manner inspiring awe)
etymology: From fear, Old English faer, sudden danger or dread, + the adverbial -ly; in David's usage the word describes not terror but the awe proper to beholding a thing made with reverent care.
biblical_def:
I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well.

David is not describing fear of his own body but the fear proper to contemplating it, the reverent dread that belongs to beholding a work whose maker's skill exceeds comprehension. Fearfully here names the quality of the workmanship, not the emotion of the one made; a thing fearfully wrought is a thing wrought with such care and power that to consider it rightly is to be struck with awe at its Maker. The verse sits inside a psalm tracing the LORD's knowledge of the unborn self, thou hast covered me in my mother's womb, so that fearfully and wonderfully made becomes David's doctrine of the body: not an accident of biology to be managed, but a handiwork deliberate enough to provoke praise. That my soul knoweth right well shows David drawing a settled conclusion, not a passing feeling; this is doctrine stated as fact, the ground of his praise rather than its occasion only. Every later theology of human dignity, every argument from the imago Dei against degrading the body, has David's fearfully as its root text: the human frame is not raw material but a work that should make the one who considers it afraid in the way only true reverence is afraid.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from FEARFUL: in a manner to produce fear or reverential awe; so as to excite dread or wonder.
webster_full: FEARFUL, a. Exciting awe or reverential dread; also, timorous, affected with fear.
FEARFULLY, adv. In a manner to excite reverential dread or awe.
Psalm 139: man is fearfully and wonderfully made, the workmanship of God.
Describes the quality of the making, not the emotion of the one made.
Grounds the doctrine of human dignity in the Maker's deliberate skill.
scriptures: I will praise thee; for I am fearfully and wonderfully made: marvellous are thy works; and that my soul knoweth right well.
corruption_summary: A culture that treats the body as raw material for self-authorship has lost precisely the reverent dread David's word names.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern body-talk, whether in cosmetic self-reinvention or in ideologies that treat sex and form as infinitely malleable, approaches the human frame as a project to be edited rather than a work already fearfully and wonderfully made.

David's doctrine stands against both the careless and the presumptuous: the body is not refuse to be despised nor clay to be endlessly re-sculpted by its own will, but a workmanship whose Maker's skill should provoke reverence before it provokes revision. Fearfully names the posture Scripture asks of us toward our own frame: not shame, not mastery, but awe.
roots_summary: From Old English faer, dread, through fearful, the -ly adverb names a quality that provokes reverent awe in the beholder, not terror in the one described.
roots_lines: Faer, Old English for sudden dread, is the deep root of fear.
Fearful names what provokes reverential awe, not mere terror.
Psalm 139 applies it to the body's own deliberate workmanship.
Marvellous are thy works stands in parallel, confirming the sense of awe.
Grounds every later doctrine of human dignity in the Maker's skill.
usage: fearfully and wonderfully made — the body as deliberate workmanship, not accident
that my soul knoweth right well — doctrine stated as settled fact
root text for the Church's doctrine of human dignity

pos: adj., comparative. (weaker; more lacking in strength)
etymology: Comparative of feeble, from Old French feble, from Latin flebilis, lamentable, from flere, to weep; a word for weakness rooted in a word for grief.
biblical_def:
But when the cattle were feeble, he put them not in: so the feebler were Laban's, and the stronger Jacob's.

The verse closes Jacob's long, uneasy contract with Laban, fourteen years of service turned into a breeding strategy that left Jacob prospering and Laban's flocks visibly diminished. On its surface it describes animal husbandry; underneath it, the text has already told us what Jacob did not fully disclose to Laban, that his success came by cunning as much as by the LORD's blessing he later claims in Genesis 31. Feebler here marks the visible outcome of an arrangement weighted, by craft or by providence or both, toward one party's increase and the other's loss. Jacob's own account to his wives afterward insists the LORD hath taken away the cattle of your father, and given them to me, folding what looks like clever breeding into divine providence. The text leaves both readings available, Jacob's partial deceit and the LORD's overruling hand, without collapsing one into the other; Scripture is comfortable narrating a man's craftiness and God's providence operating in the same event without excusing the former by the latter. The feebler and the stronger divide, two flocks under one sky, becomes an early picture of how the LORD's purposes can ride on top of, without ever sanctifying, a man's own schemes.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from FEEBLE: comparative degree; weaker; wanting strength in a greater degree than another.
webster_full: FEEBLE, a. Weak; infirm; wanting strength or vigor.
FEEBLER is its comparative: weaker than another.
Genesis 30: the feebler cattle were Laban's, the stronger Jacob's.
Marks the visible result of Jacob's long contract with Laban.
Narrated alongside Jacob's own later claim of the LORD's providence in the matter.
scriptures: But when the cattle were feeble, he put them not in: so the feebler were Laban's, and the stronger Jacob's.
corruption_summary: No live postmodern redefinition attaches; the recoverable principle is Scripture's refusal to let providence excuse craftiness.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Feebler has simply become an uncommon word, replaced by weaker in ordinary speech.

The principle in the narrative is still instructive: the LORD's blessing on Jacob's increase did not require, and does not retroactively sanctify, every method by which Jacob pursued it. A modern believer tempted to read providential success as proof that the means used to get it were therefore godly should read Genesis 30 and 31 together, and note how carefully the text keeps the two apart.
roots_summary: From Latin flebilis, lamentable, through Old French feble, feeble names a weakness the comparative -er measures against a stronger counterpart.
roots_lines: Flebilis, Latin for lamentable, lies behind feeble through Old French feble.
Feeble names a want of strength; feebler, its comparative degree.
Genesis 30 divides Laban's flocks and Jacob's by exactly this measure.
Jacob's own later words credit the LORD's providence for the increase.
The text narrates craft and providence together without equating them.

pos: adj., comparative. (more violent or vehement; harsher in manner or speech)
etymology: Comparative of fierce, from Old French fers, from Latin ferus, wild, untamed; the comparative measures one party's vehemence against another's.
biblical_def:
And the words of the men of Judah were fiercer than the words of the men of Israel.

The verse closes a bitter exchange in the uneasy days just after David's restoration to the throne following Absalom's revolt, when the men of Israel and the men of Judah contend over who has the greater claim on bringing the king home. Fiercer measures not weapons but words, a rivalry of honor between tribes that had, only recently, fought on opposite sides of a civil war. That the contention is verbal rather than physical does not make it minor; this very quarrel is the kindling for Sheba's rebellion in the very next chapter, proof that fierce words between brothers are rarely contained to words for long. The text is notably even-handed, it does not say Judah was in the right, only that Judah's words were fiercer, more vehement, pressed harder, in an argument that itself reveals wounded pride on both sides over proximity to the king rather than any principle worth the cost of further bloodshed. Scripture's realism here is instructive: a kingdom just reunited under its rightful king can still fracture again over nothing nobler than who gets credit for loyalty, and the comparative fiercer marks exactly the moment reconciliation tips back toward rupture.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from FIERCE: comparative degree; more vehement, violent, or harsh than another.
webster_full: FIERCE, a. Vehement in temper; violent; ferocious.
FIERCER is its comparative: more vehement than another.
2 Samuel 19: the words of Judah were fiercer than the words of Israel.
Describes a rivalry of honor, not a battle, in the tribes' contention over David.
The kindling for Sheba's rebellion in the very next chapter.
scriptures: And the men of Israel answered the men of Judah, and said, We have ten parts in the king, and we have also more right in David than ye: why then did ye despise us, that our advice should not be first had in bringing back our king? And the words of the men of Judah were fiercer than the words of the men of Israel.
corruption_summary: No live postmodern redefinition attaches; the recoverable principle is how quickly wounded pride between brothers escalates toward fracture.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Fiercer has not been redefined, only displaced by more intense in common speech.

The narrative behind it remains a sober warning for any body, a family, a church, a nation, newly reconciled: the words that reopen a wound are rarely the great principles, but the small comparative grievances, who gets more credit, whose loyalty is honored first. Judah and Israel had just finished a civil war and were already arguing their way back toward one, and fiercer marks precisely that turn.
roots_summary: From Latin ferus, wild or untamed, through Old French fers, fierce names an untamed vehemence; the comparative measures it between two parties.
roots_lines: Ferus, Latin for wild or untamed, is the deep root of fierce.
Fierce names vehemence; fiercer, its comparative, measures it against another's.
2 Samuel 19 applies it to Judah's words against Israel's, after David's restoration.
The quarrel is over honor and proximity to the king, not principle.
It becomes the kindling for Sheba's rebellion in the following chapter.
usage: the words of the men of Judah were fiercer — a rivalry of honor, not arms
kindling for the next chapter's rebellion under Sheba
a reunited kingdom fracturing again over wounded pride, not principle

pos: n. (a refiner of metals; one who purifies silver or gold by fire)
etymology: Agent noun from fine, to refine or purify, from Old French fin, from Latin finire, to finish, bring to completion; a finer is one whose trade is bringing metal to its finished purity.
biblical_def:
Take away the dross from the silver, and there shall come forth a vessel for the finer.

Solomon's proverb pictures the ancient refiner's trade with exact craft: dross, the base and worthless matter mixed in with the ore, must be removed before the silver underneath can be shaped into anything a finer would call a finished vessel. The proverb sits beside the one just before it, take away the wicked from before the king, and the pairing is deliberate, removing corruption from a court is the same kind of work as removing dross from silver, necessary before either produces something fit for its purpose. The finer does not create the silver's value; he only removes what obscures it, applying fire and skill until the base matter is gone and the true metal can be worked. This becomes one of Scripture's steadiest pictures of sanctification: the LORD is repeatedly cast as a refiner of silver, purifying His people in a furnace not to destroy them but to bring them, like the finer's vessel, to a use they could not serve while the dross remained. The proverb's quiet lesson is that purity is not natural to ore; it is produced, by fire and by a skilled hand willing to apply it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from FINE, v.: one who refines metal, separating the dross from silver or gold by fire.
webster_full: FINE, v.t. To refine; to purify, as metal, by separating it from dross.
FINER, n. One whose occupation is to refine metals.
Proverbs 25: removing dross from silver yields a vessel for the finer.
Paired with removing the wicked from before a king, the same kind of necessary work.
A standing picture of the LORD's sanctifying work as a refiner of His people.
scriptures: Pro 25:4
Take away the dross from the silver, and there shall come forth a vessel for the finer.
corruption_summary: No live postmodern redefinition attaches; the recoverable principle is that purity is produced by fire, not assumed by nature.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Finer survives mainly as a comparative adjective now, its older sense as the refiner's own trade name having faded from common use.

The proverb's doctrine is worth recovering against any theology of sanctification that expects holiness without heat: the silver does not purify itself, and the finer's fire is not punishment but process, the necessary means by which base matter becomes a vessel fit for use. A faith that wants the finished vessel while refusing the refiner's furnace has misunderstood both.

roots_lines: Finire, Latin for to finish, underlies fine through Old French fin.
To fine is to refine metal by removing its dross.
A finer is the tradesman who performs this refining by fire.
Proverbs 25 pairs this trade with removing corruption from a king's court.
Scripture repeatedly casts the LORD as a refiner purifying His people the same way.
usage: a vessel for the finer — the purpose purified silver is finally fit to serve
paired with removing the wicked from before a king
a standing picture of sanctification as refining by fire

pos: n. (work done by the hands; a maker's own craftsmanship)
etymology: From Old English handgeweorc, hand + work, literally the work of the hands; the oldest English word for a craftsman's own, undelegated labor.
biblical_def:
The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork.

David opens Psalm 19 with the oldest argument for a Maker: the heavens need no human witness to testify, they declare on their own, continually and without speech, and the firmament sheweth his handywork, the sky itself displaying the unmistakable craftsmanship of the hand that made it. Handywork is deliberately intimate; it is not the LORD's decree or His word only but His own hand's labor, as a craftsman's handiwork bears the unmistakable mark of the one who shaped it. The psalm moves immediately from this general revelation in creation to special revelation in the law, the heavens declare, but the law of the LORD is perfect, converting the soul, implying that the same God who left His handywork legible in the sky left a fuller, clearer word in Scripture for those who need more than the sky can say. Paul draws precisely this line in Romans, that which may be known of God is manifest, for God hath shewed it, so that men are without excuse before a Maker whose handywork in creation already testifies, even before the gospel is preached, that He is, and that He is to be glorified.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from HAND + WORK: work performed by the hands; a product of one's own immediate labor or skill.
webster_full: HANDYWORK, n. Work done by the hand; manufacture.
Applied in Scripture to creation itself as the work of God's own hand.
Psalm 19: the firmament sheweth his handywork, declaring the Maker's glory.
Paired in the same psalm with the perfect law of the LORD, special revelation.
Grounds Paul's argument in Romans that creation leaves mankind without excuse.
scriptures: Psa 19:1
To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David. The heavens declare the glory of God; and the firmament sheweth his handywork.
corruption_summary: A materialist age reads the same sky David read and credits it to chance rather than to the Hand the Psalm insists it declares.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern naturalism treats the ordered heavens as a brute fact requiring no maker, impressive only as an accident of physics, precisely the conclusion Psalm 19 and Romans 1 say the evidence itself forecloses.

David's word resists the substitution: handywork names craftsmanship, not coincidence, and a universe this legible is, on Scripture's own account, not neutral evidence awaiting interpretation but a continual declaration already understood by every observer, which is exactly why Paul can say men are without excuse rather than merely under-informed.
roots_summary: From Old English handgeweorc, hand plus work, the word names labor done directly by the hand, not delegated or indirect.
roots_lines: Handgeweorc, Old English for hand-work, is the word's root.
It names labor performed by the hand itself, not delegated.
Psalm 19 applies it to the heavens as God's own craftsmanship.
Paired with the perfect law of the LORD as a fuller revelation.
Underlies Paul's argument in Romans that creation leaves none without excuse.
usage: the firmament sheweth his handywork — creation as the Maker's own craftsmanship
paired with the perfect law of the LORD in the same psalm
the root text behind Romans 1's argument from general revelation

pos: n. (iniquity or wrong beheld; a cause of grief or complaint)
etymology: From Old French grevance, from grever, to burden or oppress, from Latin gravare, to make heavy; the word names a weight laid on the one who beholds it, not only on the one who suffers it.
biblical_def:
Why dost thou shew me iniquity, and cause me to behold grievance? for spoiling and violence are before me: and there are that raise up strife and contention.

Habakkuk opens his prophecy not with praise but with a question the LORD does not immediately answer: why must the prophet himself behold grievance, the iniquity, violence, and lawless contention overrunning Judah, while crying out and receiving no apparent response. Grievance here is not Habakkuk's own complaint against God but the wrong he is made to witness in his own people, a burden laid specifically on the one who sees it rightly. The honesty of the opening is itself part of Scripture's theology of lament: Habakkuk does not pretend not to see what he sees, and he does not treat his unanswered cry as evidence against the LORD's justice, but as the opening half of a conversation that by chapter two yields the LORD's famous answer, the just shall live by his faith. Grievance names exactly the painful middle of faithful watching, after the wrong is seen clearly and before the answer comes, which is where a great deal of the believer's actual life, under governments, in churches, in a fallen world, is actually lived.
webster_summary: Webster (1828), from GRIEVE: that which causes grief; a burden, wrong, or iniquity beheld or endured.
webster_full: GRIEVE, v.t. To afflict with pain of mind; to cause sorrow or grief.
GRIEVANCE, n. That which causes grief; a wrong or oppression suffered or beheld.
Habakkuk 1: the prophet is caused to behold grievance, violence, and strife in his own land.
Names the burden of rightly seeing wrong, not only of suffering it directly.
Opens a prophecy that by its second chapter yields the LORD's famous answer.
scriptures: Hab 1:3
Why dost thou shew me iniquity, and cause me to behold grievance? for spoiling and violence are before me: and there are that raise up strife and contention.
corruption_summary: Modern grievance culture has repurposed the word for an identity to perform rather than a wrong to lament before God, inverting Habakkuk's pattern.
corruption_paragraphs: Contemporary usage has made grievance a social category, a status conferred by claimed victimhood and displayed for standing rather than brought before God for an answer, so that the having of a grievance becomes its own kind of currency rather than the opening half of an honest lament.

Habakkuk's pattern corrects this at the root: he names the grievance plainly, without flattering his own perception of it, and then waits on the LORD rather than organizing around it. The prophet's grievance ends in faith, the just shall live by his faith; a grievance that never intends to reach that answer, that exists only to be aired, has stopped at the first half of Habakkuk's book and refused the second.
roots_summary: From Latin gravare, to make heavy, through Old French grevance, the word names a weight laid on the one who beholds a wrong, not only on its direct victim.
roots_lines: Gravare, Latin for to make heavy, lies behind grevance and grievance.
It names the weight of a wrong beheld, not only one suffered directly.
Habakkuk 1 applies it to the prophet's own burden in watching his nation's sin.
The complaint is honest, unflattering, and addressed directly to the LORD.
It opens a book that ends in the LORD's answer: the just shall live by his faith.
